Arrange Pyth

GeometryAreaTriangles
Game: Two equal squares are cut into pieces, and the pieces are put back in a different order. There is nothing to win: the story the pieces tell never changes.
How to play: Drag the round point along the bottom line of the left square, or focus it and use the left and right arrow keys. Press Midpoint or Reset for another starting point.

Look for the math

The same four pieces sit inside both squares. Only the red pieces change: one large red square on the left, two smaller ones on the right. That is the whole proof.

Four triangles and a square

Let the bottom edge of the left square be split into lengths a and b by the point M. The square's side is a + b. The applet cuts out four right triangles, each with legs a and b. What is left in the middle is a square whose side is the third side c of those triangles. So the left square has area c² + 4·(a·b/2).

Now put the triangles back

The right square holds the very same four triangles. The space they leave is two squares, one of side a and one of side b, with areas a² and b². Taking the four matching triangles away from both equal squares leaves c² = a² + b²: the Pythagorean theorem, made visible as a dissection rather than a page of algebra.

Every position works

Move M anywhere along the edge and a + b stays the same. The four triangles change shape, but the two rearrangements still match, so the identity holds for every split. The logic test checked all 111 whole-pixel positions of the applet's own 500 by 300 canvas, many other canvas sizes, and compared every drawn point with a second reading of the applet's code. The claim is true. One honesty note: the applet rounds canvas coordinates to whole pixels, so on a canvas whose height minus the square's side is odd, its outline is a pixel too tall and the drawn pieces carry a tiny sliver. This page uses the applet's 500 by 300 canvas, where every pixel lands exactly. The applet calls itself Proof #36 while its page's Explanation link points to Proof #9; we follow the page's rearrangement.

Drag M almost to an end of the edge. One triangle becomes very thin and the other very fat, but the two red areas still add up.
